content.text:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `normalize` or `resolve`, reads UTF-8 text from standard input, and writes one result line per input line to standard output. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every remaining line is a record, including an empty one. Exit 0 when every record succeeds.

In `normalize` mode each record is one URI reference and its output line is the normalized form. In `resolve` mode each record is a base URI, one space, and a reference; the output line is the reference resolved against the base and then normalized. The first space separates the two, so a reference may contain spaces and a base may not.

Parse a URI reference into scheme, authority, path, query and fragment by RFC 3986's generic syntax: an optional scheme running to the first `:`, which may not be preceded by any `/`, `?` or `#`; an optional authority introduced by `//` and running to the next `/`, `?` or `#`; the path up to the next `?` or `#`; an optional query from `?` to the next `#`; an optional fragment from `#` to the end. An absent component and an empty one are different, so `http://a/b?` has an empty query, `http://a/b` has none, and both print back the way they came. Inside an authority the userinfo is everything before the last `@`, the port is everything after the first `:` that follows the last `]`, and the host is what lies between.

Normalization applies in this order. Lowercase the scheme, using ASCII rules only. Normalize percent-encodings in every component: uppercase the two hexadecimal digits of each `%XX`, then replace the triplet with the character it encodes when that character is unreserved, meaning one of `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `-`, `.`, `_` and `~`. Lowercase the host, using ASCII rules only and leaving the userinfo alone. Drop the port when it is written empty or written with exactly the digits of the scheme's default, which is 80 for `http` and `ws`, 443 for `https` and `wss`, and 21 for `ftp`; no other scheme has one, and a port padded with a leading zero is not written with those digits and stays. Remove dot segments from the path by RFC 3986 section 5.2.4, so a `.` segment disappears, a `..` segment removes the segment before it, and a `..` that would climb above the root is discarded. Finally, when an authority is present and the path is empty, make the path `/`. Dot removal never touches the query or the fragment.

Resolve by RFC 3986 section 5.2.2 in its strict form, in which a reference that repeats the base's scheme is still an absolute URI. A reference that writes a scheme is itself the target, with the dot segments removed from its path. A reference that writes an authority takes the base's scheme and keeps everything else of its own. A reference with neither and an empty path takes the base's authority and path, takes the base's query only when it writes no query of its own, and takes its own fragment, which may be absent. Otherwise, when the reference's path does not start with `/`, merge it onto the base's: keep everything of the base path up to and including its last `/`, or use the reference path alone when the base path holds no `/`, except that a base that has an authority and an empty path contributes a single leading `/`. Remove the dot segments from the resulting path, take the base's authority and the reference's query and fragment, and normalize the whole.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js normalize|resolve` when the arguments are not exactly one of the two mode words; `error: line N: expected a base and a reference` when a `resolve` record holds no space; `error: line N: the base has no scheme` when the base of a `resolve` record writes no scheme; and `error: line N: the path has a truncated percent-encoding` when a `%` is not followed by two hexadecimal digits, with `path` replaced by `userinfo`, `host`, `query` or `fragment` for whichever component carries it, those five being checked in that order. N counts records from 1. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

{
  "id": "code:uri-resolve",
  "tier": 5,
  "domain": "parsing",
  "title": "Resolve and normalize URI references by RFC 3986",
  "prompt": "`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `normalize` or `resolve`, reads UTF-8 text from standard input, and writes one result line per input line to standard output. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every remaining line is a record, including an empty one. Exit 0 when every record succeeds.\n\nIn `normalize` mode each record is one URI reference and its output line is the normalized form. In `resolve` mode each record is a base URI, one space, and a reference; the output line is the reference resolved against the base and then normalized. The first space separates the two, so a reference may contain spaces and a base may not.\n\nParse a URI reference into scheme, authority, path, query and fragment by RFC 3986's generic syntax: an optional scheme running to the first `:`, which may not be preceded by any `/`, `?` or `#`; an optional authority introduced by `//` and running to the next `/`, `?` or `#`; the path up to the next `?` or `#`; an optional query from `?` to the next `#`; an optional fragment from `#` to the end. An absent component and an empty one are different, so `http://a/b?` has an empty query, `http://a/b` has none, and both print back the way they came. Inside an authority the userinfo is everything before the last `@`, the port is everything after the first `:` that follows the last `]`, and the host is what lies between.\n\nNormalization applies in this order. Lowercase the scheme, using ASCII rules only. Normalize percent-encodings in every component: uppercase the two hexadecimal digits of each `%XX`, then replace the triplet with the character it encodes when that character is unreserved, meaning one of `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `-`, `.`, `_` and `~`. Lowercase the host, using ASCII rules only and leaving the userinfo alone. Drop the port when it is written empty or written with exactly the digits of the scheme's default, which is 80 for `http` and `ws`, 443 for `https` and `wss`, and 21 for `ftp`; no other scheme has one, and a port padded with a leading zero is not written with those digits and stays. Remove dot segments from the path by RFC 3986 section 5.2.4, so a `.` segment disappears, a `..` segment removes the segment before it, and a `..` that would climb above the root is discarded. Finally, when an authority is present and the path is empty, make the path `/`. Dot removal never touches the query or the fragment.\n\nResolve by RFC 3986 section 5.2.2 in its strict form, in which a reference that repeats the base's scheme is still an absolute URI. A reference that writes a scheme is itself the target, with the dot segments removed from its path. A reference that writes an authority takes the base's scheme and keeps everything else of its own. A reference with neither and an empty path takes the base's authority and path, takes the base's query only when it writes no query of its own, and takes its own fragment, which may be absent. Otherwise, when the reference's path does not start with `/`, merge it onto the base's: keep everything of the base path up to and including its last `/`, or use the reference path alone when the base path holds no `/`, except that a base that has an authority and an empty path contributes a single leading `/`. Remove the dot segments from the resulting path, take the base's authority and the reference's query and fragment, and normalize the whole.\n\nA failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js normalize|resolve` when the arguments are not exactly one of the two mode words; `error: line N: expected a base and a reference` when a `resolve` record holds no space; `error: line N: the base has no scheme` when the base of a `resolve` record writes no scheme; and `error: line N: the path has a truncated percent-encoding` when a `%` is not followed by two hexadecimal digits, with `path` replaced by `userinfo`, `host`, `query` or `fragment` for whichever component carries it, those five being checked in that order. 1: /**
2:  * URI reference parsing, normalization and resolution per RFC 3986,
3:  * following the simplified generic-syntax rules laid out in the task
4:  * specification.
5:  */
6: 
7: export class PercentError extends Error {
8:   constructor(component) {
9:     super(`truncated percent-encoding in ${component}`)
10:     this.component = component
11:   }
12: }
13: 
14: const HEX_RE = /[0-9A-Fa-f]/
15: 
16: function isHex(ch) {
17:   return HEX_RE.test(ch)
18: }
19: 
20: function isUnreservedByte(code) {
21:   return (
22:     (code >= 0x41 && code <= 0x5a) || // A-Z
23:     (code >= 0x61 && code <= 0x7a) || // a-z
24:     (code >= 0x30 && code <= 0x39) || // 0-9
25:     code === 0x2d || // -
26:     code === 0x2e || // .
27:     code === 0x5f || // _
28:     code === 0x7e // ~
29:   )
30: }
31: 
32: /**
33:  * Parse a URI reference into { scheme, authority, path, query, fragment }.
34:  * Absent components are `null`; present-but-empty ones are `''`.
35:  * `authority` is the raw (unsplit) authority string, or null when absent.
36:  */
37: export function parseRef(s) {
38:   let rest = s
39:   let scheme = null
40: 
41:   const colonIdx = rest.indexOf(':')
42:   if (colonIdx !== -1) {
43:     const before = rest.slice(0, colonIdx)
44:     if (!/[/?#]/.test(before)) {
45:       scheme = before
46:       rest = rest.slice(colonIdx + 1)
47:     }
48:   }
49: 
50:   let authority = null
51:   if (rest.startsWith('//')) {
52:     const rem = rest.slice(2)
53:     const m = rem.search(/[/?#]/)
54:     if (m === -1) {
55:       authority = rem
56:       rest = ''
57:     } else {
58:       authority = rem.slice(0, m)
59:       rest = rem.slice(m)
60:     }
61:   }
62: 
63:   let pathEnd = rest.length
64:   const qIdx = rest.indexOf('?')
65:   const hIdx = rest.indexOf('#')
66:   if (qIdx !== -1 && qIdx < pathEnd) pathEnd = qIdx
67:   if (hIdx !== -1 && hIdx < pathEnd) pathEnd = hIdx
68: 
69:   const path = rest.slice(0, pathEnd)
70:   let remainder = rest.slice(pathEnd)
71: 
72:   let query = null
73:   if (remainder.startsWith('?')) {
74:     const h2 = remainder.indexOf('#')
75:     if (h2 === -1) {
76:       query = remainder.slice(1)
77:       remainder = ''
78:     } else {
79:       query = remainder.slice(1, h2)
80:       remainder = remainder.slice(h2)
81:     }
82:   }
83: 
84:   let fragment = null
85:   if (remainder.startsWith('#')) {
86:     fragment = remainder.slice(1)
87:   }
88: 
89:   return { scheme, authority, path, query, fragment }
90: }
91: 
92: /**
93:  * Split a raw authority string into { userinfo, host, port }.
94:  * `userinfo` and `port` are `null` when absent.
95:  */
96: export function parseAuthority(a) {
97:   let userinfo = null
98:   let hostport = a
99:   const atIdx = a.lastIndexOf('@')
100:   if (atIdx !== -1) {
101:     userinfo = a.slice(0, atIdx)
102:     hostport = a.slice(atIdx + 1)
103:   }
104: 
105:   const bracketIdx = hostport.lastIndexOf(']')
106:   const searchFrom = bracketIdx === -1 ? 0 : bracketIdx
107:   const colonIdx = hostport.indexOf(':', searchFrom)
108: 
109:   let host, port
110:   if (colonIdx !== -1) {
111:     host = hostport.slice(0, colonIdx)
112:     port = hostport.slice(colonIdx + 1)
113:   } else {
114:     host = hostport
115:     port = null
116:   }
117:   return { userinfo, host, port }
118: }

120: /** Uppercase %XX digits, decoding unreserved bytes. Throws PercentError. */
121: function normalizePercent(s, component) {
122:   let out = ''
123:   for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) {
124:     const c = s[i]
125:     if (c === '%') {
126:       if (i + 2 >= s.length || !isHex(s[i + 1]) || !isHex(s[i + 2])) {
127:         throw new PercentError(component)
128:       }
129:       const hex = s.slice(i + 1, i + 3).toUpperCase()
130:       const code = parseInt(hex, 16)
131:       if (isUnreservedByte(code)) {
132:         out += String.fromCharCode(code)
133:       } else {
134:         out += '%' + hex
135:       }
136:       i += 2
137:     } else {
138:       out += c
139:     }
140:   }
141:   return out
142: }

146:   ws: '80',
147:   https: '443',
148:   wss: '443',

152: /** Remove dot segments from a path per RFC 3986 5.2.4. */
153: export function removeDotSegments(path) {
154:   let input = path
155:   let output = ''
156:   while (input.length > 0) {
157:     if (input.startsWith('../')) {
158:       input = input.slice(3)

169:     } else if (input === '/..') {

171:       const idx = output.lastIndexOf('/')

187:   for (const ch of s) {
188:     const code = ch.codePointAt(0)

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `normalize` or `resolve`, reads UTF-8 text from standard input, and writes one result line per input line to standard output. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every remaining line is a record, including an empty one. Exit 0 when every record succeeds.

In `normalize` mode each record is one URI reference and its output line is the normalized form. In `resolve` mode each record is a base URI, one space, and a reference; the output line is the reference resolved against the base and then normalized. The first space separates the two, so a reference may contain spaces and a base may not.

Parse a URI reference into scheme, authority, path, query and fragment by RFC 3986's generic syntax: an optional scheme running to the first `:`, which may not be preceded by any `/`, `?` or `#`; an optional authority introduced by `//` and running to the next `/`, `?` or `#`; the path up to the next `?` or `#`; an optional query from `?` to the next `#`; an optional fragment from `#` to the end. An absent component and an empty one are different, so `http://a/b?` has an empty query, `http://a/b` has none, and both print back the way they came. Inside an authority the userinfo is everything before the last `@`, the port is everything after the first `:` that follows the last `]`, and the host is what lies between.

Normalization applies in this order. Lowercase the scheme, using ASCII rules only. Normalize percent-encodings in every component: uppercase the two hexadecimal digits of each `%XX`, then replace the triplet with the character it encodes when that character is unreserved, meaning one of `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `-`, `.`, `_` and `~`. Lowercase the host, using ASCII rules only and leaving the userinfo alone. Drop the port when it is written empty or written with exactly the digits of the scheme's default, which is 80 for `http` and `ws`, 443 for `https` and `wss`, and 21 for `ftp`; no other scheme has one, and a port padded with a leading zero is not written with those digits and stays. Remove dot segments from the path by RFC 3986 section 5.2.4, so a `.` segment disappears, a `..` segment removes the segment before it, and a `..` that would climb above the root is discarded. Finally, when an authority is present and the path is empty, make the path `/`. Dot removal never touches the query or the fragment.

Resolve by RFC 3986 section 5.2.2 in its strict form, in which a reference that repeats the base's scheme is still an absolute URI. A reference that writes a scheme is itself the target, with the dot segments removed from its path. A reference that writes an authority takes the base's scheme and keeps everything else of its own. A reference with neither and an empty path takes the base's authority and path, takes the base's query only when it writes no query of its own, and takes its own fragment, which may be absent. Otherwise, when the reference's path does not start with `/`, merge it onto the base's: keep everything of the base path up to and including its last `/`, or use the reference path alone when the base path holds no `/`, except that a base that has an authority and an empty path contributes a single leading `/`. Remove the dot segments from the resulting path, take the base's authority and the reference's query and fragment, and normalize the whole.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js normalize|resolve` when the arguments are not exactly one of the two mode words; `error: line N: expected a base and a reference` when a `resolve` record holds no space; `error: line N: the base has no scheme` when the base of a `resolve` record writes no scheme; and `error: line N: the path has a truncated percent-encoding` when a `%` is not followed by two hexadecimal digits, with `path` replaced by `userinfo`, `host`, `query` or `fragment` for whichever component carries it, those five being checked in that order. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. From each line strip the leading spaces and tabs; ignore the line when nothing is left or when what is left begins with `#`. Otherwise the address runs to the next space or tab or to the end of the line, one run of spaces and tabs is skipped, and the rest of the line, verbatim, is the cell's content. Exit 0 whenever the sheet parses.

An address is one or two letters naming a column and one to three digits naming a row, upper-cased when read, so `a1` and `A1` are one cell; columns run `A` to `Z` and then `AA` to `ZZ`, and the row is at least 1. Cells print in ascending column order and, within a column, ascending row order.

Content that begins with `=` is a formula; anything else is a literal. A literal that is empty, or a cell nobody declared, is the number 0. A literal that matches an optional `-`, digits, and optionally a `.` and more digits is that number. A literal that is exactly one of the error tokens `#DIV/0!`, `#REF!`, `#VALUE!`, `#CYCLE!`, `#NAME?` and `#ERR!` is that error. Everything else is text.

A formula body holds numbers written as digits with an optional `.` and more digits and no sign and no exponent, cell addresses, ranges written `A1:B3`, the bare words `TRUE` and `FALSE`, function calls, parentheses, and the operators `^`, `*`, `/`, `+`, `-`, `=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Spaces and tabs may sit anywhere between tokens. Names are read case-insensitively. Precedence, loosest first, is the comparisons, then `+` and `-`, then `*` and `/`, then `^`, and then a leading `-` or `+`; the comparisons and the additive and multiplicative operators group to the left, `^` groups to the right, and a leading sign binds tighter than `^`, so `-2^2` is 4 and `2^3^2` is 512. Anything the grammar does not accept makes the cell `#ERR!`, and so does a range written anywhere but directly as a function argument.

The functions are `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `COUNT` and `AVG`, each taking one or more arguments, `ABS` taking exactly one, and `IF` taking exactly three. A call with the wrong number of arguments is `#ERR!` and a call to any other name is `#NAME?`. An argument that is a range contributes every cell it covers, in ascending column and then ascending row order, whichever corner it was written from. `SUM` totals, `MIN` and `MAX` pick, `AVG` totals and divides by how many values it saw, and `COUNT` reports how many of its values are numbers. `IF` reads its first argument as a condition, taking `TRUE` and a non-zero number as true and `FALSE` and zero as false, and returns only the branch it takes, so an error in the other branch is invisible.

A value is a number, text, a boolean, or an error. In an arithmetic position a boolean is 1 or 0 and text is `#VALUE!`. Division by a zero divisor is `#DIV/0!`, and so is any arithmetic result that is not finite. A comparison compares two numbers numerically, two texts by code point, and two booleans with false below true; across kinds every number is below every text and every text is below every boolean. An address outside the addressable range is `#REF!`. A cell whose evaluation reaches itself, directly or through other cells, is `#CYCLE!`. An error reaching an operator or a function is the result: for an operator the left operand's error wins over the right one's, and for a function the first error among the arguments read left to right, ranges expanded, wins over everything else, including over `COUNT` counting.

A name, a route prefix and an event key are each one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/`, `:` and `-`. Every count is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without a leading zero unless it is exactly `0`.

`bucket <name> <capacity> <refill> <per>` declares a token bucket, with a capacity of at least 1, a refill of at least 0, and a period of at least 1. `window <name> <limit> <span>` declares a sliding window, with a limit of at least 0 and a span of at least 1. Two policies may not share a name. `route <prefix> <policy>...` sends every key that starts with that prefix to those policies, in the order written; every policy must already be declared, and two routes may not share a prefix. `event <tick> <key>` is one arrival at that tick, and ticks never go backwards across the file. Once the first event appears no further `bucket`, `window` or `route` line may follow.

Each policy keeps one independent state per key. A key is limited by the route whose prefix it starts with and which is longest among those that match; a key no route matches is always allowed. When an event arrives, every policy on its route first advances to the event's tick, then every one of them is asked, and only when all of them allow it does each of them record it. A denied event changes no policy's stored allowance.

A token bucket holds `capacity` tokens and starts full when a key first reaches it. Advancing it to a tick adds `refill` tokens for every `per` ticks that passed since it last advanced for that key, without ever passing the capacity, and partial periods accumulate exactly: after `n` ticks the bucket holds `refill` times `n` divided by `per` more tokens than it did, and that fraction is never rounded away. It allows a request when it holds at least one whole token, and recording one spends exactly one.

A sliding window remembers the ticks of the requests it recorded for a key. Advancing it to a tick forgets every remembered tick at or before the tick minus the span, so the window covers the `span` ticks ending at the current one. It allows a request when fewer than `limit` ticks remain remembered, and recording one remembers this tick.

`replay` prints one line per event in log order: `<tick> <key> allow`, or `<tick> <key> deny <policy>` naming the first policy on the route, in the order the route wrote them, that refused. `summary` instead prints `<key> allowed=<a> denied=<d>` for every key that saw an event, in ascending key order, and then `total allowed=<a> denied=<d>`.

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `replay` or `summary`, and reads a limiter file from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace. Exit 0 whenever the file parses.

A name, a route prefix and an event key are each one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/`, `:` and `-`. Every count is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without a leading zero unless it is exactly `0`.

`bucket <name> <capacity> <refill> <per>` declares a token bucket, with a capacity of at least 1, a refill of at least 0, and a period of at least 1. `window <name> <limit> <span>` declares a sliding window, with a limit of at least 0 and a span of at least 1. Two policies may not share a name. `route <prefix> <policy>...` sends every key that starts with that prefix to those policies, in the order written; every policy must already be declared, and two routes may not share a prefix. `event <tick> <key>` is one arrival at that tick, and ticks never go backwards across the file. Once the first event appears no further `bucket`, `window` or `route` line may follow.

Each policy keeps one independent state per key. A key is limited by the route whose prefix it starts with and which is longest among those that match; a key no route matches is always allowed. When an event arrives, every policy on its route first advances to the event's tick, then every one of them is asked, and only when all of them allow it does each of them record it. A denied event changes no policy's stored allowance.

A token bucket holds `capacity` tokens and starts full when a key first reaches it. Advancing it to a tick adds `refill` tokens for every `per` ticks that passed since it last advanced for that key, without ever passing the capacity, and partial periods accumulate exactly: after `n` ticks the bucket holds `refill` times `n` divided by `per` more tokens than it did, and that fraction is never rounded away. It allows a request when it holds at least one whole token, and recording one spends exactly one.

A sliding window remembers the ticks of the requests it recorded for a key. `src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `values` or `deps`, and reads a sheet from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. From each line strip the leading spaces and tabs; ignore the line when nothing is left or when what is left begins with `#`. Otherwise the address runs to the next space or tab or to the end of the line, one run of spaces and tabs is skipped, and the rest of the line, verbatim, is the cell's content. Exit 0 whenever the sheet parses.

An address is one or two letters naming a column and one to three digits naming a row, upper-cased when read, so `a1` and `A1` are one cell; columns run `A` to `Z` and then `AA` to `ZZ`, and the row is at least 1. Cells print in ascending column order and, within a column, ascending row order.

Content that begins with `=` is a formula; anything else is a literal. A literal that is empty, or a cell nobody declared, is the number 0. A literal that matches an optional `-`, digits, and optionally a `.` and more digits is that number. A literal that is exactly one of the error tokens `#DIV/0!`, `#REF!`, `#VALUE!`, `#CYCLE!`, `#NAME?` and `#ERR!` is that error. Everything else is text.

A formula body holds numbers written as digits with an optional `.` and more digits and no sign and no exponent, cell addresses, ranges written `A1:B3`, the bare words `TRUE` and `FALSE`, function calls, parentheses, and the operators `^`, `*`, `/`, `+`, `-`, `=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Spaces and tabs may sit anywhere between tokens. Names are read case-insensitively. Precedence, loosest first, is the comparisons, then `+` and `-`, then `*` and `/`, then `^`, and then a leading `-` or `+`; the comparisons and the additive and multiplicative operators group to the left, `^` groups to the right, and a leading sign binds tighter than `^`, so `-2^2` is 4 and `2^3^2` is 512. Anything the grammar does not accept makes the cell `#ERR!`, and so does a range written anywhere but directly as a function argument.

The functions are `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `COUNT` and `AVG`, each taking one or more arguments, `ABS` taking exactly one, and `IF` taking exactly three. A call with the wrong number of arguments is `#ERR!` and a call to any other name is `#NAME?`. An argument that is a range contributes every cell it covers, in ascending column and then ascending row order, whichever corner it was written from. `SUM` totals, `MIN` and `MAX` pick, `AVG` totals and divides by how many values it saw, and `COUNT` reports how many of its values are numbers. `IF` reads its first argument as a condition, taking `TRUE` and a non-zero number as true and `FALSE` and zero as false, and returns only the branch it takes, so an error in the other branch is invisible.

A value is a number, text, a boolean, or an error. In an arithmetic position a boolean is 1 or 0 and text is `#VALUE!`. Division by a zero divisor is `#DIV/0!`, and so is any arithmetic result that is not finite. A comparison compares two numbers numerically, two texts by code point, and two booleans with false below true; across kinds every number is below every text and every text is below every boolean. An address outside the addressable range is `#REF!`. A cell whose evaluation reaches itself, directly or through other cells, is `#CYCLE!`. An error reaching an operator or a function is the result: for an operator the left operand's error wins over the right one's, and for a function the first error among the arguments read left to right, ranges expanded, wins over everything else, including over `COUNT` counting.

`values` prints `<address>=<value>` for every declared cell. A number prints as JavaScript would print it after being rounded to ten significant digits, an error prints as its token, a boolean prints as `TRUE` or `FALSE`, and text prints as itself. `deps` instead prints `<address>:` followed by ` <address>` for every distinct cell the content names directly, ranges expanded, ordered by column and then by row; a literal, and a formula that does not parse, name none.

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `values` or `deps`, and reads a sheet from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. From each line strip the leading spaces and tabs; ignore the line when nothing is left or when what is left begins with `#`. Otherwise the address runs to the next space or tab or to the end of the line, one run of spaces and tabs is skipped, and the rest of the line, verbatim, is the cell's content. Exit 0 whenever the sheet parses.

An address is one or two letters naming a column and one to three digits naming a row, upper-cased when read, so `a1` and `A1` are one cell; columns run `A` to `Z` and then `AA` to `ZZ`, and the row is at least 1. Cells print in ascending column order and, within a column, ascending row order.

Content that begins with `=` is a formula; anything else is a literal. A literal that is empty, or a cell nobody declared, is the number 0. A literal that matches an optional `-`, digits, and optionally a `.` and more digits is that number. A literal that is exactly one of the error tokens `#DIV/0!`, `#REF!`, `#VALUE!`, `#CYCLE!`, `#NAME?` and `#ERR!` is that error. Everything else is text.

A formula body holds numbers written as digits with an optional `.` and more digits and no sign and no exponent, cell addresses, ranges written `A1:B3`, the bare words `TRUE` and `FALSE`, function calls, parentheses, and the operators `^`, `*`, `/`, `+`, `-`, `=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Spaces and tabs may sit anywhere between tokens. Names are read case-insensitively. Precedence, loosest first, is the comparisons, then `+` and `-`, then `*` and `/`, then `^`, and then a leading `-` or `+`; the comparisons and the additive and multiplicative operators group to the left, `^` groups to the right, and a leading sign binds tighter than `^`, so `-2^2` is 4 and `2^3^2` is 512. Anything the grammar does not accept makes the cell `#ERR!`, and so does a range written anywhere but directly as a function argument.

The functions are `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `COUNT` and `AVG`, each taking one or more arguments, `ABS` taking exactly one, and `IF` taking exactly three. A call with the wrong number of arguments is `#ERR!` and a call to any other name is `#NAME?`. An argument that is a range contributes every cell it covers, in ascending column and then ascending row order, whichever corner it was written from. `SUM` totals, `MIN` and `MAX` pick, `AVG` totals and divides by how many values it saw, and `COUNT` reports how many of its values are numbers. `IF` reads its first argument as a condition, taking `TRUE` and a non-zero number as true and `FALSE` and zero as false, and returns only the branch it takes, so an error in the other branch is invisible.

A value is a number, text, a boolean, or an error. In an arithmetic position a boolean is 1 or 0 and text is `#VALUE!`. Division by a zero divisor is `#DIV/0!`, and so is any arithmetic result that is not finite. A comparison compares two numbers numerically, two texts by code point, and two booleans with false below true; across kinds every number is below every text and every text is below every boolean. An address outside the addressable range is `#REF!`. A cell whose evaluation reaches itself, directly or through other cells, is `#CYCLE!`. An error reaching an operator or a function is the result: for an operator the left operand's error wins over the right one's, and for a function the first error among the arguments read left to right, ranges expanded, wins over everything else, including over `COUNT` counting.

`values` prints `<address>=<value>` for every declared cell. A number prints as JavaScript would print it after being rounded to ten significant digits, an error prints as its token, a boolean prints as `TRUE` or `FALSE`, and text prints as itself. `deps` instead prints `<address>:` followed by ` <address>` for every distinct cell the content names directly, ranges expanded, ordered by column and then by row; a literal, and a formula that does not parse, name none.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js values|deps` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, `error: line N: invalid cell address <address>`, and `error: line N: cell <address> is declared twice`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.
